Although the initial motivation for this project, which emerged from a series of informal conversations among the team members during the fifth semester about the difficulty that hostel students face when attempting to keep track of what they eat on a daily basis, was fairly modest, the scope gradually expanded as we realised that the problem of recognising Indian food items in photographs, where several dishes are typically served together on a single plate and frequently overlap or mix with one another, is considerably harder than the single-dish classification problem that most of the existing literature, being largely based on Western datasets such as Food-101, has addressed. Consequently, after experimenting for nearly a month with a classification network that, despite reaching reasonable accuracy on cropped images of individual dishes, failed almost entirely on full plates, we decided, partly on the advice of our guide and partly because of a paper on single-stage detectors that one of us had read for a different course, to reformulate the task as object detection, which in turn required us to collect and annotate our own dataset of roughly seven hundred photographs taken in the canteen, the mess and our homes.
